content: The antiproton, often denoted as p-bar, is the antiparticle counterpart of the proton. While antiprotons are inherently stable, they are typically short-lived in practice because any collision with a proton results in mutual annihilation, releasing a burst of energy. Antiprotons were first discovered in 1955 by physicists Emilio Segrè and Owen Chamberlain at the University of California, Berkeley. This groundbreaking discovery earned them the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1959. Structurally, an antiproton is composed of two anti-up quarks and one anti-down quark. The creation of antiprotons requires an immense amount of energy, equivalent to a temperature of 10 trillion Kelvin (10¹³ K). Such conditions are not naturally occurring outside of the Big Bang. However, at CERN, antiprotons are artificially produced by accelerating protons in the Proton Synchrotron to an energy of 26 GeV and then colliding them with an iridium rod. These high-energy collisions generate a variety of particles and antiparticles, including antiprotons, which are subsequently isolated using magnetic fields in a vacuum. The mass of an antiproton is identical to that of a proton, approximately 1836 times the mass of an electron. This equivalence in mass necessitates further research into the fundamental differences between matter and antimatter to explain why the universe, following the Big Bang, predominantly consists of matter, with very little antimatter remaining in our solar system. Antiprotons have been detected in cosmic rays for over 25 years, initially through balloon-borne experiments and more recently via satellite-based detectors. Their presence in cosmic rays is attributed to collisions between cosmic ray protons and interstellar nuclei, which produce secondary antiprotons. These antiprotons propagate through the galaxy, confined by galactic magnetic fields. Their energy spectrum is influenced by collisions with interstellar atoms and by potential losses as they escape the galaxy. Current measurements of the antiproton cosmic ray energy spectrum align with the standard model of their production through cosmic ray collisions. This data places upper limits on the number of antiprotons that could arise from exotic sources, such as the annihilation of supersymmetric dark matter particles or the evaporation of primordial black holes. It also provides a lower limit on the antiproton lifetime, estimated to be between 1 and 10 million years. Since the galactic storage time for antiprotons is approximately 10 million years, any intrinsic decay would alter their galactic residence time and distort the observed cosmic ray antiproton spectrum. The properties of antiprotons are predicted by CPT symmetry, a fundamental principle of quantum field theory. According to CPT symmetry, the mass and lifetime of an antiproton should be identical to those of a proton, while its electric charge and magnetic moment should be equal in magnitude but opposite in sign. No violations of CPT symmetry have ever been observed. Several experiments have been conducted to detect cosmic ray antiprotons. These include balloon-borne experiments such as BESS (flown in 1993, 1995, and 1997), CAPRICE (flown in 1994), and HEAT (flown in 2000). Space-based experiments include AMS, a prototype flown on the space shuttle in 1998 and intended for the International Space Station, and PAMELA, a satellite experiment launched in June 2006 to detect cosmic rays and antimatter. Antiprotons are routinely produced at Fermilab for use in collider physics experiments at the Tevatron, where they are collided with protons. The use of antiprotons in such experiments allows for higher average collision energies between quarks and antiquarks compared to proton-proton collisions. This is because the valence quarks in protons and the valence antiquarks in antiprotons tend to carry the largest fraction of their respective particle's momentum.
